title: Jews in the Islamic world
hook: Baghdad, Cairo, Kairouan: long periods of flourishing, and times of hardship

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saadia Gaon, who put the Torah into Arabic and argued that faith and reason lead to one truth. Your line was faith and reason. Today, the world he wrote from.

Kitab. It's the Arabic word for a book. Saadia's great work of philosophy has it in its Arabic title, and it shows up in a phrase the Qur'an uses for Jews and Christians: ahl al-kitab, the people of the book, or as one old translation puts it, the People of the Scripture. In the copies of Saadia's book that came down to us, kitab is spelled in Hebrew letters. Arabic words, Hebrew script: that way of writing is called Judeo-Arabic, a small window into a very big world. For centuries, from Baghdad to Cairo to Kairouan, Jewish life unfolded in lands ruled by Muslims, and in Arabic.
screen: `KITAB: A BOOK.` → `PEOPLE OF THE BOOK.` → `ARABIC WORDS, HEBREW LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The academies we've been following, Sura and Pumbedita, came to sit in a world governed by Muslim rulers, whose capital was Baghdad. Under Islamic law, Jews and Christians were usually treated as protected peoples, called dhimmi. They could keep their faith, their courts and their houses of worship. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits, and how those limits felt depended a great deal on who was in power. There were long stretches of flourishing. Jews worked as merchants, doctors, scholars and officials. They wrote poetry, philosophy and Bible commentary in Arabic, and their letters crossed seas because trade routes did. Jewish thinkers read Muslim philosophers and argued with them; ideas moved in both directions. That's the world Saadia wrote from. There were also hard times. In Cairo, for a time, a caliph ordered synagogues and churches torn down, before the policy was reversed. Some rulers enforced humiliating rules. Communities sometimes faced violence, and some had to flee. Both are true, and the honest history keeps both: neither perfect harmony nor constant persecution fits what the records show. Neighbors, business partners, rivals, sometimes victims, sometimes friends, living the long middle of history side by side, and writing it down in Arabic, in Hebrew letters.
screen: `PROTECTED, AND LIMITED.` · `LONG STRETCHES OF FLOURISHING.` · `AND TIMES OF HARDSHIP.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Say one Judeo-Arabic word quietly a few times: kitab, a book, which can be spelled in Arabic letters or in Hebrew ones, the way Saadia's book spells it. Let it open a picture: a woman in Kairouan writing to her brother, in Arabic in Hebrew letters, about a wedding, a sick child, the price of bread, two languages in one line. Hold that picture without deciding what it means, and if you pray, you can remember the people of that world.
Dhimmi. The status of Jews and Christians as protected peoples under Islamic law, free to keep their faith but taxed and limited.
Your line: jews among muslims. The long story is bigger than any one picture. Day nine hundred fourteen, in the books.

howItsDone: Jewish communities with roots in North Africa, the Middle East and Yemen keep traditions, melodies and words from centuries of life in Arabic-speaking lands, and Judeo-Arabic texts are still studied.

chat.says: Were Jews in the old Muslim world always treated well, or always persecuted?
options: Neither always: protected but limited, with flourishing times and hard times too.
Always well: there were no limits, and every ruler treated them alike.
Always persecuted: they were never allowed to keep their own courts.
chat.meaning: Dhimmi status protected faith, courts and worship, with a special tax and limits; the records show long flourishing and real hardship.

dhimmi.meaning: protected peoples under Islamic law, taxed and limited

kitab.meaning: the Arabic word for a book

Kairouan.meaning: a North African city with a Jewish community

sources.work: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions

notes: 'People of the Scripture' is attributed to 'one old translation' (Pickthall 1930); the phrase is not put in quotation marks. Confirm.

Dhimmi status (protection, own courts and worship, special tax/jizya, limits varying by ruler) is summarized generally; a Keeper and a historian should check the framing for fairness to both Jews and Muslims.
Hardship example: the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim's orders to destroy synagogues and churches in Egypt, later reversed. Not named in the voice; confirm.
'For centuries' is used without a count. 'Sura and Pumbedita came to sit near Baghdad' (the academies moved to Baghdad later in the Gaonic period); confirm.
Judeo-Arabic spelling of kitab as כתאב; confirm.
This day touches another tradition: it names Islam only as neighbor and ruler, ranks no one, and keeps both flourishing and hardship. Please check tone.

Editor: 'Now here's the twist' cut; claims that Saadia himself wrote in Hebrew letters now say his book has come down in Hebrew letters (teach, practice, myth, fork reveal); the practice's Cairo merchant writing about a shipment became a woman in Kairouan so it doesn't anticipate day 915's merchant-and-late-ship hook.

Auditor: "Sura and Pumbedita ... near the city of Baghdad" was geographically loose (Sura lay well to the south; the academies relocated to Baghdad only late in the Gaonic period); now says the rulers' capital was Baghdad.
